lesson.title: Taming a Wild Gain: Negative Feedback
lesson.summary: Feeding a fraction of the op-amp's output back to its inverting input creates a self-correcting loop that forces the two inputs to nearly the same voltage, replacing the op-amp's huge and unpredictable open-loop gain with a stable, resistor-set closed-loop gain.
lesson.body:
The op-amp output chapter ended on a problem: an open-loop gain in the hundreds of thousands means only a few hundred microvolts of input difference is enough to saturate the output against a supply rail. That makes an open-loop op-amp nearly useless for ordinary amplification, since real input signals are almost always larger than a few hundred microvolts. Negative feedback is the fix, and it works by routing a portion of the output back to the inverting input.

Here is why "negative" is the right word for it. Suppose, in some circuit, the output voltage were to rise for any reason. If a fraction of that rising output is fed back to V-, then V- rises too. But recall from the inverting input chapter that a rising V- pushes the output down, opposing, or negating, the very increase that caused it in the first place. The loop fights its own changes and settles into equilibrium rather than running away. That equilibrium condition, when the loop gain (the open-loop gain multiplied by the feedback fraction) is large, is well approximated by V- being pulled to almost exactly the same voltage as V+, a condition often called the virtual short.

Work through the classic non-inverting amplifier to see this in action. Apply Vin = 1 V directly to V+. Connect a resistor R1 = 1 kilohm from V- down to ground, and a feedback resistor Rf = 9 kilohms from the output back to that same V- node. Feedback theory gives the closed-loop gain directly: Gain = 1 + Rf/R1 = 1 + 9000/1000 = 1 + 9 = 10, so Vout = 10 x 1 V = 10 V. Now verify that using the virtual short idea instead, without invoking the gain formula at all. Since V- is forced to nearly equal V+ = 1 V, the current flowing down through R1 to ground is I = V-/R1 = 1 V / 1000 ohms = 0.001 A, 1 milliamp. Because an ideal op-amp input draws essentially no current, that same 1 milliamp has to flow through Rf as well, arriving from the output. So Vout = V- + I x Rf = 1 V + (0.001 A x 9000 ohms) = 1 V + 9 V = 10 V, exactly matching the formula. Both routes to the answer agree, which is exactly the kind of cross-check worth doing whenever a new circuit idea is introduced.

Negative feedback does more than just set a predictable gain, it also makes that gain far less sensitive to the op-amp's own open-loop gain, which varies significantly between individual devices and with temperature. Using the exact closed-loop relationship Vout/Vin = Aol / (1 + Aol x beta), where beta = R1/(R1+Rf) = 1000/10000 = 0.1 for the circuit above, compare Aol = 100,000 against Aol = 500,000, a fivefold difference. At Aol = 100,000: Vout/Vin = 100,000 / (1 + 100,000 x 0.1) = 100,000 / 10,001 = 9.999. At Aol = 500,000: Vout/Vin = 500,000 / (1 + 500,000 x 0.1) = 500,000 / 50,001 = 9.9998. Despite a fivefold swing in the underlying open-loop gain, the closed-loop gain barely moves, both values round to 10.00. That desensitization, not merely the convenience of a resistor-set gain, is the real reason negative feedback is used in nearly every linear op-amp circuit: it trades an enormous, unreliable open-loop gain for a modest, precisely controlled closed-loop gain set by two resistors the designer chooses.
